5 PMAC I/O AND MEM-
ORY MAP 
Introduction 
  Certain registers that are 
under the PMAC automatic con-
trol can cause problems if the 
user writes to them directly -- 
particularly those used in the 
servo calculations. 
This guide to the PMAC memory and input and output registers is provided 
for user reference.  The PMAC architecture is very open, allowing the user to 
examine and use many internal registers for his own use.  Usually this is done 
through the use of M-variables, which point to locations in the memory-I/O 
space of the PMAC processor.  Once defined to point to the proper location, an 
M-variable can be treated as any other variable for reading and writing.  
 
The PMAC processor is the Motorola 56001 DSP.  The 56001 has dual data buses, each 24 bits wide, so that both 
operands in a calculation may be brought in simultaneously.  Each bus has access to a 16-bit address space (0000hex 
to FFFFhex), which provides 65,536 24-bit words.  One bus and address space is called 'X', and the other is called 
'Y'.  Therefore, when specifying a single-word memory location, one must use 'X:' or 'Y:' with the 16-bit address.  
the PMAC input and output is mapped into the same address space with the memory. 
 
PMAC uses double-word memory for both extended fixed-point values and for floating-point values (single words 
are always fixed point).  In this memory map, the fixed-point double-word locations are specified by a 'D:' (double), 
and the floating-point double-word locations are specified by an 'L:' (long).  This matches the syntax of M-variable 
declarations for these registers.  If an address is specified without any prefix, it means that a special internal format 
is used to hold data in that word.  
 
The user may specify PMAC addresses with either decimal or hexadecimal values; the hex values must be preceded 
by a '$' to be interpreted as hex.  For example, Y:$FFC0 is the hexadecimal specification, and Y:65472 is the 
decimal specification of the same word address. 
 
M-variables are defined by providing the word address, the offset, the width, and the format (irrelevant for bits).  
Refer to M-variables in the manual for details of the definition.  Several M-variables were defined at the factory to 
match to inputs and outputs.  For instance, M11 thru M18 were assigned to Machine Inputs 1 thru 8 (MI1-MI8), and 
M1 to M8 were assigned to Machine Outputs 1 thru 8 (MO1-MO8).   
 
Example statements that did this are as follows: 
 
M11->Y:$FFC2,0,1 (Mach. In. 1: Offset 0, width 1)  
M1->Y:$FFC2,8,1 (Mach. Out. 1: Offset 8, width 1) 
M162->D:$002C (Motor #1 Actual Position: fixed pt.) 
M163->L:$081F (C.S. 1 X-axis Position: floating pt.)

Motor and Coordinate System Status and Control Registers 
The addresses given in this section are for Motor 1 and Coordinate System 1.  Table headers for each set of 16 regis-
ters give the starting addresses of the set for each Motor/C.S.  For the register of another Motor x or C.S. x, add (x-
1)*$C0 or (x-1)*192 to the appropriate Motor 1 or C.S. 1 address. 
 
Example 
For the Motor 4 target position register, by the table compute $0A40 + ($080B-$0800) = $0A4B.  By formula, com-
pute (4-1)*$C0 + $080B = $0A4B

Gate Array Registers (PMAC[1] Specific) 
The registers in the PMAC "DSPGATE" Gate-Array ICs are mapped into the memory space of the PMAC proces-
sor.  Each DSPGATE contains four consecutively numbered channels; there may be up to 4 DSPGATEs in a PMAC 
system, for up to 16 channels.  Every PMAC contains DSPGATE 1, which has channels 1 through 4.  If Option 1 is 
ordered (not available on PMAC-Lite), DSPGATE 2 is provided, which has channels 5 through 8.  If Accessory 24 
is ordered (not available on PMAC-STD), DSPGATE 3 is provided, which has channels 9 through 12.  If Accessory 
24 Option 1 is ordered as well (not available on PMAC-STD), DSPGATE 4 is provided, which has channels 13 
through 16.

DSPGATE1 Registers (PMAC2 Specific) 
 
Remarks 
 
Channels 1-4, residing in the first DSPGATE1 IC, are present on all PMAC2 boards.   
Channels 5-8, residing in the second DSPGATE1 IC, are present on PMAC2 boards with Option 1.   
Channels 9-12, residing in the third DSPGATE1 IC, are present on PMAC2 systems with a 4-channel PMAC2 
ACC-24 daughter board (not available as of this writing).   
Channels 13-16, residing in the fourth DSPGATE1 IC, are present on on PMAC2 systems with an 8-channel ACC-
24 daughter board (not available as of this writing).

PMAC Example Programs 
 
Example 1: Suggested M-variable Definitions (PMAC[1] Specific) 
 
This file contains a suggested set of M-Variable definitions.  These definitions can be very useful for getting access 
to important I/O and registers.  It is not required that you use these particular definitions.  Most example programs 
will use these definitions. 
 
CLOSE  
M0..1023->*  
; To ensure commands are on-line 
; To clear all existing definitions 
M0->X:$0,0,24,U ; Servo cycle counter 
 ; General Purpose inputs and outputs  
; (PMAC-PC,-Lite,-VME)  
M1->Y:$FFC2,8,1 ; Machine Output 1 
M2->Y:$FFC2,9,1 ; Machine Output 2 
M3->Y:$FFC2,10,1 ; Machine Output 3 
M4->Y:$FFC2,11,1 ; Machine Output 4 
M5->Y:$FFC2,12,1 ; Machine Output 5 
M6->Y:$FFC2,13,1 ; Machine Output 6 
M7->Y:$FFC2,14,1 ; Machine Output 7 
M8->Y:$FFC2,15,1 ; Machine Output 8 
M9->Y:$FFC2,8,8,U ; Machine Outputs 1-8 treated as byte 
M11->Y:$FFC2,0,1 ; Machine Input 1 
M12->Y:$FFC2,1,1 ; Machine Input 2 
M13->Y:$FFC2,2,1 ; Machine Input 3 
M14->Y:$FFC2,3,1 ; Machine Input 4 
M15->Y:$FFC2,4,1 ; Machine Input 5 
M16->Y:$FFC2,5,1 ; Machine Input 6 
M17->Y:$FFC2,6,1 ; Machine Input 7 
M18->Y:$FFC2,7,1 ; Machine Input 8 
M19->Y:$FFC2,0,8,U ; Machine Inputs 1-8 treated as byte 
 ; Control-Panel Port Input Bits (so can be used as general 
 ; I/O if I2=1) (These definitions valid for PMAC-PC,  
 ; -Lite, & -VME)

Example 1:  Suggested M-Variable Definitions (PMAC2 Specific) 
 
  These are only sugges-
tions; the user is free to make 
whatever definitions are desired. 
This file contains suggested definitions for M-variables on the PMAC2.  It is 
similar to the file for the PMAC(1) family of boards, but there are significant 
differences in the input/output definitions, both for servo registers and general-
purpose I/O.

Example 2:  A Simple Move 
This example shows how to program a simple move on the PMAC.  First the program specifies how to do the move, 
then commands the move. 
 
;******************** Set-up and Definitions ******************** 
&1 ; Coordinate System 1 
CLOSE ; Make sure all buffers are closed 
#1->X ; Assign motor 1 to the X-axis - 1 program unit 
 ; of X is 1 encoder count of motor #1 
 
;******************** Motion Program Text *********************** 
OPEN PROG 1 ; Open buffer for program entry, Program #1 
CLEAR ; Erase existing contents of buffer 
LINEAR ; Blended linear interpolation move mode 
ABS ; Absolute mode - moves specified by position 
TA500 ; Set 1/2 sec (500 msec) acceleration time 
TS0 ; Set no S-curve acceleration time 
F5000 ; Set feedrate (speed) of 5000 units (cts)/sec 
X10000 ; Move X-axis to position 10000 
DWELL500 ; Stay in position for 1/2 sec (500 msec) 
X0 ; Move X-axis to position 0 
CLOSE ; Close buffer - end of program 
To run this program:  
&1 B1 R ; Coordinate System 1, point to Beginning of  
; Program 1, Run

Example 3:  A More Complex Move 
This example introduces incremental and time-specification of moves, looping logic, using variables, scaling of 
axes, and simple arithmetic.  Note that logical and mathematical operations do not delay moves. 
 
;******************** Set-up and Definitions ******************** 
&2 ; Coordinate system 2 
 ; NOTE: No motor can be simultaneously defined 
 ; in more than one coordinate system 
CLOSE ; Make sure all buffers are closed 
#5->1000X ; 1 unit (cm) of X is 1000 counts of motor 5 
;******************** Motion Program Text *********************** 
OPEN PROG 2 ; Open buffer for entry, Program #2 
CLEAR ; Erase existing contents of buffer 
LINEAR ; Blended linear interpolation move mode 
INC ; Incremental mode - m oves specified by distance 
TA500 ; 1/2 sec (500 msec) acceleration time 
TS250 ; 1/4 sec in each half of S-curve 
P1=0 ; Initialize a loop counter variable 
WHILE (P1<10) ; Loop until condition is false (10 times) X10 
 ; Move X-axis 10 cm (=10,000 cts) positive  
 ; DWELL500 
Hold position for 1/2 sec X-10 
 ; Move X-axis back 10 cm negative DWELL500 
 ; Hold position for 1/2 sec  
P1=P1+1  
 ; Increment loop counter 
ENDWHILE ; End of loop 
CLOSE ; Close buffer - end of program 
To run this program:  
&2 B2 R ; Coordinate System 2, point to Beginning of  
; Program 2, Run

Example 6:  A Simple G-Code Program 
 
 The part program does not 
need to know how the G-codes 
and M-codes are executed. 
This is a simple example of a PMAC G-Code program.  Gxx is interpreted as 
a call to label Nxx000 of PROG 1000 (below).  Mxx is interpreted as a call 
to label Nxx000 of PROG 1001 (bottom).  Far more extensive codes are 
possible;  standard forms of the common codes are provided on diskette. 
 
 
 
 
;******************** Part Program Text ************************** 
OPEN PROG 5 CLEAR ; Prepare motion program 5 for entry 
G17 G90 ; XY plane, absolute move spec 
G97 S1800 ; Set spindle speed of 1800 rpm 
F500 ; Cutting speed 500 mm/min 
G00 X10.00 Y5.00 ; Rapid move to (10, 5) 
M03 ; Start spindle 
G04 P2.0 ; Wait 2 seconds 
G01 Z0 ; Lower cutter 
X30.25 Y5.00 ; Linear XY move 
G03 X35.25 Y10.00 J5 ; CCW arc move 
G01 X35.25 Y50.10 ; Linear move 
G03 X30.25 Y55.10 I-5 ; CCW arc move 
G01 X10.00 Y55.10 ; Linear move 
G03 X5.00 Y50.10 J-5 ; CCW arc move 
G01 X5.00 Y10.00 ; Linear move 
G03 X10.00 Y5.00 I5 ; CCW arc move 
G01 Z5 M05 ; Cutter up, stop 
G00 X0 Y0 ; Back to home 
CLOSE  
;***************************************************************** 
Motion program 1000 contains the G-Code subroutines 
OPEN PROG 1000 CLEAR ; Prepare buffer 1000 for entry 
RAPID RETURN ; G00 Rapid mode (N0 is implied) 
N01000 LINEAR RETURN ; G01 Linear interpolation mode 
N02000 CIRCLE1 RETURN ; G02 Clockwise circle mode 
N03000 CIRCLE2 RETURN ; G03 Counterclockwise circle mode 
N04000 READ(P) ; G04 Dwell for P seconds 
IF (Q100 & 32768 > 0) ; P parameter specified? 
 DWELL (Q116*1000) ; PMAC specifies dwell time in msec 
ENDIF  
RETURN  
N17000 NORMAL K-1 RET ; G17 Specify XY plane 
N18000 NORMAL J-1 RET ; G18 Specify ZX plane 
N19000 NORMAL I-1 RET ; G19 Specify YZ plane 
N90000 ABS RET ; G90 Absolute mode 
N91000 INC RET ; G91 Incremental mode 
N97000 READ(S) ; G97 Spindle speed set 
IF (Q100 & 262144 > 0) ; S parameter specified?  
 I422=Q119/30 ; #4 jog speed in cts/msec 
ENDIF  
RETURN  
CLOSE

Example 7:  A Robotic Application 
 
This example shows how a robotic style application can be implemented very quickly and easily on the PMAC.  
This example uses the Option 2 dual-ported RAM to pass values in the fastest possible manner.  (The normal com-
munications port could be used at a slight cost in performance.)  Here, the host PC is performing the inverse kine-
matic calculations every 5 msec, converting tip positions to joint positions and passing the joint positions to the 
DPRAM, where they are accessed as M-variables.  PMAC interpolates between these intermediate points on each 
axis with a cubic spline that is updated every servo cycle. 
 
;******************** Set-up and Definitions ******************** 
CLOSE ; Make sure all buffers are closed 
&1 ; Define axes (joints) in degrees in  
; Coordinate System 1 
#1->1024X ; 1024 cts/deg 
#2->2000Y ; 2000 cts/deg 
#3->2000Z ; 2000 cts/deg 
#4->5000A ; 5000 cts/deg 
#5->512B ; 512 cts/deg 
#6->277.77778C ; 277.77778 cts/deg 
M70->F:$D200 ; 32-bit  IEEE floating-point format 
M71->F:$D201 ; variables in DPRAM for passing joint 
M72->F:$D202 ; positions to PMAC.  The host writes 
M73->F:$D203 ; to these locations through the use 
M74->F:$D204 ; of pointer variables. 
M75->F:$D205 ;  
M113->X:$C000,13,1 ; Interrupt bit to signal host for next set of points 
;******************** Motion Program Text *********************** 
OPEN PROG 75 CLEAR  
SPLINE1 ; Cubic spline mode 
TA5 ; Set spline segment time of 5 msec 
INC ; Incremental mode 
X0 Y0 Z0 A0 B0 C0 ; First zero-distance move 
X0 Y0 Z0 A0 B0 C0 ; Second zero-distance move 
ABS ; Further moves will be absolute 
WHILE (P1>0) ; Host sets P1 to exit this mode 
 X(M70) Y(M71) Z(M72) A(M73) B(M74) C(M75) M113=1 M113=0 
 ; Calculate next segment, signal host 
 ; thru interrupt for more data 
ENDWHILE  
CLOSE  
 To run this program: 
&1 B75 R ;Coordinate System 1, point to Beginning of 
;  Program 75, Run

 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-31 
Example 8:  Rotary Tangent to X-Y System 
 
This example shows how easy it is to keep a rotary axis tangent (or normal) to the movement of an X-Y system.  
The rotary axis is controlled by a separate program running simultaneously that monitors X-Y variables.  The XY 
part program DOES NOT need to know anything about the rotary axis - it is all automatic. 
 
;*********************  Set-up and Definitions ******************** 
CLOSE   
&1 #1->10000X ; Motor 1 is X axis in Coordinate system 1 
#2->10000Y ; Motor 2 is Y axis in Coordinate system 1 
&2 #3->40C ; Motor 3 is C axis in Coordinate system 2 
I15=0 ; Do trig calculations in degrees 
I327=14400 ; C axis rolls over every 14400 cts 
M161->D:$0028 ; Motor 1 present commanded position 
M163->D:$080B ; Motor 1 target position 
M261->D:$0064 ; Motor 2 present commanded position 
M263->D:$08CB ; Motor 2 target position 
P10=3072 ; 1 count in Mx61, Mx63 units (div by 0 check) 
;************** Motion Program Text for Rotary Axis **************** 
OPEN PROG 10 CLEAR  
SPLINE1 TA20 ; Cubic spline segments of 20 msec 
WHILE (P1>0) ; As long as in this mode 
 Q0=M163-M161 ; X target position - X current position 
 Q1=M263-M261 ; Y target position - Y current position 
 IF (ABS(Q0)>P10 OR ABS(Q1)>P10) ; Target position < > current position? 
 Q2=ATAN2(Q1) ; Calculate angle - ATAN2 (Q1, Q2) 
 ENDIF  
 C(Q2) ; Move rotary axis to new angle 
ENDWHILE   
CLOSE  
 
Example 9:  PLC Input Programming 
This example shows how to use a PLC program to create customized inputs.  As the PLC program repeatedly cycles 
in background, it checks the input lines and issues commands as appropriate.  This program shows how to use a 
thumbwheel input line to create a jog switch dedicated to a particular motor.  Note the use of a "latching flag" so that 
commands are only given on a change of state, making them edge triggered. 
;********************* Set-up and Definitions ******************** 
CLOSE  
M50->Y:$FFC1,0 ; Thumbwheel port input bit 0 
M60->* ; Latching bit for M50 
;********************* PLC Program Text ************************** 
OPEN PLC 16  
CLEAR  
IF (M50=1) ; Motor 1 jog plus switch on 
 IF (M60=0) ; But not on last time 
 COMMAND"#1J+" ; Issue command 
 M60=1 ; Set latching flag 
 ENDIF  
ELSE ; Motor 1 jog plus switch off 
 IF (M60=1) ; But not off last time 
 COMMAND"#1J/" ; Issue stop command 
 M60=0 ; Set latching flag 
 ENDIF  
ENDIF  
CLOSE

3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-32
Example 10:  PLC Display Programming 
 
This example shows how a PLC can be used to continually update a display with values derived from the current 
status.  Here, the program takes the actual motor positions on an R-Theta table, converts them to X-Y positions, puts 
them in the dual-ported RAM for the host, and on the LCD display. 
 
;********************* Set up and Definitions *********************   
CLOSE  
#1->-100U+15000 ; Radial arm at 100 cts/mm; offset 150 mm 
#2->40C ; Rotary axis at 40 cts/deg 
M162->D:$002B ; Motor 1 actual position 
M262->D:$0067 ; Motor 2 actual position 
M100->F:$D400 ; DPRAM register for X position reporting 
M200->F:$D401 ; DPRAM register for Y position reporting 
;********************* PLC Program Text ***************************   
OPEN PLC 6 CLEAR  
P162=150-M162/(I108*32*100) ; Radial distance from center in mm 
P262=M262/(I208*32*40) ; Rotary position in degrees 
M100=P162*COS(P262) ; X position in mm => DPRAM register 
M200=P162*SIN(P262) ; Y position in mm => DPRAM register 
DISPLAY 5,10.2,M100 ; Formatted display to LCD 
DISPLAY 15,10.2,M200 ; Formatted display to LCD 
CLOSE  
 
Example 11:  Precision Slaving 
This example shows how the PMAC can use an external time-base source for sophisticated precision slaving appli-
cations.  Here it is used for multiple-pass screw threading on a lathe with an open-loop spindle.  Coil winding appli-
cations are virtually identical as are cut-on-the-fly applications for conveyorized or extruded material.  The PMAC 
slaves its cutter axes (X&Z) to an encoder on the spindle so that cutter speed tracks spindle speed, resulting in con-
stant pitch.  This is done simply in time-base mode.  Define a "real-time" speed for the master (spindle) and set the 
time-base constant based on this.  Write the program for the slave axes as if the master were always operating at the 
real-time speed.  The time base control will compensate automatically for changes in the spindle speed. 
 
;********************* Set-up and Definitions ********************* 
&1 ; Define axes in Coordinate System 1 
#1->10000X ; Motor 1 is X at 10000 cts/in (radial) 
#2->10000Z ; Motor 2 is Z at 10000 cts/in (traverse) 
 
Spindle encoder has 1024 lines/rev or 4096 cts/rev.  At real-time speed of 
3000 rpm (50 rps), encoder frequency is 204.8 cts/msec.  By formula, the time 
base constant is 131,072/204.8 = 640. 
 
WY:1833,640 ; Set time base constant (at address 1833) 
I193=1833 ; Tell Coordinate System 1 to use this  
 ; address as the time-base source. 
 
;********************* Motion Program Text ************************ 
 
This program is written to cut a 5-pitch (5 threads per inch) screw.  It as-
sumes the spindle speed is 3000 rpm, or 50 rps.  Cutting speed is therefore 
50(rev/sec)/5(rev/in)=10 in/sec.  Programmed time for each loop must be an 
exact multiple of 20 msec for cutter to match thread each pass (50rev/sec <=> 
20msec/rev). 

===== PDF PAGE 511 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-33 
OPEN PROG 77 CLEAR ; Prepare buffer 77 for entry 
P100=3.00 ; X (radial) dimension of outside of stock 
P101=P100 ; Starting location of cut 
RAPID X(P100-0.1) Z2 ; Move quickly to starting position 
WHILE (P101<3.10) ; Loop until 0.1 inches deep 
 P101=P101+0.01 ; Increase depth 0.01 inch 
 TM100 ; 100 msec "plunge" time 
 X(P101) ; Radial axis into stock ("plunge") 
 TM(24*1000/10) ; 24 inches at 10 in/sec (in msec) 
 Z26 ; Make threading pass for 24 inches (26-2) 
 TM60 ; 60 msec retract time 
 X(P100-0.1) ; Retract to just outside of stock 
 TM(24*1000/30) ; 24 inches at 30 in/sec (in msec) 
 Z2 ; Reverse move for next pass 
 ; Total time for moves in loop is 
 ; 100+2400+60+800=3360 msec, which is an 
 ; exact multiple of 20 msec, or 1 spindle rev. 
ENDWHILE ; End of loop  
RAPID X0 Z0 ; Return to home position 
CLOSE  
 
Example 12: Matching Positions on the Fly 
 
This example shows how the position-capture function of PMAC can be used to match positions on the fly with a 
moving system not under PMAC control.  This particular example has a short belt that takes items arriving at un-
even intervals and evens out the spacing to place them between the lugs of a conveyor belt driven by a variable-
speed drive.  The same technique is applicable to any application requiring the matching of position of two moving 
devices when the spacing is not exactly known ahead of time. 
 
The application makes use of PMAC's hardware position-capture registers, which register the position on an external 
trigger to the count, regardless of speed.  This permits very high speed registration and correction.  The belt in this 
application would probably also be slaved to the lugged conveyor in time-base mode (see Example 10) for speed 
matching -- this would keep any position corrections relatively small. 
 
 
 
 
;***************** Set-up and Definitions ****************************** 
CLOSE  
&1 #1->X ; Motor 1 is X-axis scaled in counts 
M11->Y:$FFC2,0,1 ; M11 is Machine Input 1 
M203->X:$C007,0,24,S ; Encoder 2 captured-position register 
M217->X:$C004,17,1 ; Encoder 2 position-capture flag 
I907=2 ; Capture ENC2 on rising edge of flag 
I908=0 ; Use HMFL2 to capture ENC2 
P1=5000 ; 5000 counts of ENC2 per lug 
P2=1325 ; "No-correction" position within lug  
 ; cycle, when captured 
;***************** Motion Program Text ******************************** 
OPEN PROG 346 CLEAR  
INC ; Incremental move mode 
SPLINE1 TA10 ; Cubic spline segments of 10 msec 
WHILE (M11=1) ; Loop once per item as long as input set 
  WHILE (M217=0) ; Loop until photocell blocked 
  X(P10) ; P10 is nominal distance in 10 msec 

===== PDF PAGE 512 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-34
  ENDWHILE ; Loop back to check for trigger again 
 ; Found trigger, so calculate and adjust 
  P3=M203 % P1 ; Read captured position of lug conveyor 
 ; and do modulo by counts per lug to find 
 ; out where in lug cycle we are. 
  P4=P3-P2 ; Compare to no-correction position -- 
 ; difference is error to make up 
  X(P10+P4/4) ; Make up first 1/4 of error in 10 msec 
  X(P10+P4/2) ; Make up 1/2 of error in 10 msec 
  X(P10+P4/4) ; Make up last 1/4 of error in 10 msec 
ENDWHILE ; Loop back for next item 
 
Example 13:  Spindle Operation 
This program provides for sophisticated spindle operation, including constant surface speed (CSS) mode.  It breaks 
the spindle move into very small pieces (25 msec in this case), so the spindle can react very quickly to the need for a 
change in velocity.  This example requires the use of Motor #1 for the X-axis as the controlling dimension for CSS 
mode.  In CSS mode, the spindle speed is varied with the radial dimension of the tool tip so that the surface speed of 
the spindle past the tool tip is constant.  Essentially, the rotational velocity of the spindle is inversely proportional to 
the radial dimension of the tool tip (the X-axis position +/- an offset).  Since this could lead to a request for infinite 
rotational velocity, there is a maximum rotational velocity -- specified by G92.  
 
The program relies on the following variables: 
 
M55  a  flag denoting whether the spindle is ON CW (= +1), ON CCW (= -1), or OFF (= 0) set 
 by part program 
P97  desired spindle speed in RPM set by part program -- absolute value 
P96  desired spindle surface speed in ft/min or m/min, set by part program (in this case  
P97 is calculated from P96) -- absolute value 
P95  maximum spindle acceleration magnitude in RPM/sec set as system constant 
P92  maximum permitted spindle velocity in RPM set in part program (G92S__) 
P93  number of segments per second for spindle program set as system constant 
M96  a flag denoting CSS mode (=1) or not (=0) set by part program 
M70  a flag denoting metric (=1) or English (=0) set by part program 
M95  a flag denoting positive accel (= +1), negative accel (= -1), or no accel (= 0) set in 
 spindle program 
 
P197  commanded spindle speed for current segment in RPM not necessarily same as desired  
 spindle speed P97, but always approaching magnitude of P97 signed value  
M162  the register holding Motor #1 (X-axis) actual position units are 1/(I108*32) encoder  
 counts 
M164  the register holding Motor #1 position offset bias 
P162  variable holding Motor #1 position converted to counts 
M191  the register holding the scaling between X-axis position in user units and Motor #1  
 position in counts set in axis definition statement 
M194  the register holding the offset between X-axis zero  position and Motor #1 zero  
 position, in counts set in axis definition statement 
P98  variable holding the difference between X-axis zero and spindle center (if any) set in 
 part program (G92R__) 
P163  variable holding the X-axis radial distance from the spindle center first motor #1  
 position is converted to axis position [(P162-M194)/M191], then the spindle center  
 offset (P98) is subtracted

 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-35 
;********************* Set-up and definitions *************************** 
P1=3.14159272 ; PI -- for angular to surface speed 
P95=1000 ; Maximum spindle accel in RPM/sec 
P93=40  ; 40 segments per second 
M55->* ; Defined as self-referenced flag 
M95->* ; Ditto 
M96->* ; Ditto 
M70->* ; Ditto 
M95->* ; Ditto 
M162->D:$002B ; Motor #1 actual position register 
 ; (was D:$002C in V1.09 and older) 
M164->D:$0813 ; Motor #1 position bias register 
M191->L:$0822 ; Motor #1 X-axis coefficient 
M194->L:$0825 ; Motor #1 offset coefficient 
;********************* Actual spindle program *************************** 
CLOSE  
OPEN PROG 1010  
CLEAR  
LINEAR ; Linear blended moves 
INC(C) ; Incremental move specification 
TM(1000/P93) ; Move segment size in msec 
TA(1000/P93) ; Accel thru entire segment 
TS0 ; Straight ramp accel 
P197=0 ; Starting RPM is zero 
WHILE (M55!=0 OR P197!=0)  
 IF (M96=1) ; Constant surface speed mode? 
  P162=ABS((M162+M164)/(I108*32 )); Motor #1 actual pos in cts 
  P163=(P162-M194)/M191-P98 ; X-axis radial distance 
  IF (ABS(P163)>0.1) ; Not  ~zero? 
   P97= P96/(2*P1*P163) ; Convert to rotational speed 
   IF (M70=0) P97=12*P97 ; English conversion (in->ft) 
  ELSE P97=1000*P97 ; Metric conversion (mm->m) 
   IF (P97>P92) ; Past limit? 
    P97=P92 ; Set to limit 
   ENDIF  
 ELSE  
   P97=P92 ; Set to RPM limit 
 ENDIF  
 ENDIF  
 IF (M55*P97<P197) M95=-1 ; Negative accel required 
  IF (M55*P97>P197) M95=1 ; Positive accel required 
   IF (M95!=0) ; Change of speed required? 
    P197=P197+M95*P95/P93 ; Slew to new RPM for this segment 
    IF ((P197-M55*P97)*M95>0) ; Past desired RPM? 
     P197=M55*P97 ; Set to desired RPM 
       M95=0 ; Mark as no longer accelerating 
      ENDIF  
    ENDIF  
  C(P197/(60*P93)) ; Actual incremental move segment 
ENDWHILE  
DWELL50  
M95=0 ; Clear accel flag to end &1 wait 
CLOSE

Example 14:  Torque-limited Velocity Move 
 
This program performs a torque-limited velocity move.  Axis moves at constant velocity as long as torque is below a 
preset limit (here measured by the DAC register, but could be an actual torque/force sensor).  If the limit is ex-
ceeded, the commanded velocity is reduced. 
 
CLOSE DELETE GATHER DELETE TRACE 
M102->Y:$C003,8,16,S      ; DAC1 register 
P102=3200 ; Torque limit 
M1=1  
OPEN PROG 47  
CLEAR  
TA10  
TS0  
TM10  
LINEAR  
INC  
P1=100 ; Nominal distance (cts) in 10 msec 
WHILE (M1=1) ; As long as in this mode 
 IF (M102<P102)   ; Within torque limit (current amp) 
 P2=P1 ; Move nominal distance 
 ELSE ; Exceeded torque limit 
 IF (P2>0)  
 P2=P2-5 ; Reduce distance 
 ELSE  
 P2=0 ; Don't let go negative 
 ENDIF  
 ENDIF  
 X(P2) ; Make next segment of move 
ENDWHILE  
CLOSE  
 
Example 15:  A Torque Limited Screwing Operation 
This example shows how to do a torque limited screwing operation.  The key is to steadily increment the screwing 
motion in small pieces until some measure of the torque exceeds a preset limit.  Here the DAC output (into a torque-
mode amplifier) is used, but an ADC input from motor current or an actual torque sensor could also be used. 
 
CLOSE  
&1  
#3->2000Z ; Vertical axis (in mm) 
#4->2000C ; Rotary axis (in turns)

 ; (indirect measure of torque)  
P102=4000 ; Torque limit (in DAC bits) 
OPEN PROG 508 CLEAR  
ABS(Z,C) ; Both axes absolute  
PSET C0 ; Call current rotary position zero 
P1=-5 ; End Z position of fast move 
TA50 ; Fast move accel time 
F10 ; Fast move speed 
Z(P1) ; Command fast move 
DWELL5 ; Momentary pause (optional) 
TA10 TM10 ; Move segment time of 10 msec in loop

P2=0 ; C-axis position index 
WHILE (P2<3.0 AND M102<P102) ; Loop until 3 turns or high torque

 P2=P2+0.1 ; Increment C-axis position 
 Z(P1) C(P2) ; Next piece of screwing move

Example 16:  Altering Destination in Moves 
 
This program allows altered destination in moves.  The card is always moving toward an X position of P1 and a Y 
position of P2, but it does it in small increments so when P1 or P2 is changed, it will change direction within a few 
milliseconds.  P1 and P2 can be changed from the host on the fly. 
 
CLOSE  
OPEN PROG 2  
CLEAR  
P9=100 ; Vector distance per increment 
P11=0 ; Starting X position 
P12=0 ; Starting Y position 
I187=10 ; C.S. 1 accel time 
I188=0 ; C.S. 1 S-curve time 
TM10 ; Increment time in msec 
WHILE (M1=1) ; Whatever condition you like 
 P21=P1-P11 ; X distance to go 
 P22=P2-P12 ; Y distance to go 
P0=SQRT(P21*P21+P22*P22) ; Vector distance to go  
IF(P0>P9) ; If longer than increment 
 P0=P9/P0 ; Fraction of distance 
 P11=P11+P21*P0 ; X increment 
 P12=P12+P22*P0 ; Y increment 
 ELSE ; Distance < increment 
 P11=P1 ; Just go to destination 
 P12=P2  
 ENDIF  
 X(P11) Y(P12) ; Make move 
ENDWHILE  
CLOSE  
Example 17:  Changing Speed  
 
This program is an example of moving at high speed until some sort of external command, then reacting very 
quickly to the command, but changing speed very slowly.  It works by splitting the move into very small segments, 
and using WHILE loops to continue in one mode until the signal is received. 
 
CLOSE  
OPEN PROG 10  
CLEAR  
P4=150000  
P5=3000  
P6=600  

===== PDF PAGE 516 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-38
INC(X) ; X-axis in incremental mode 
TM(P5/P6) ; move segment time (5 msec here!) 
TA(P5/P6) ; accel time (<= TM) 
P3=P4/(P6*P6) ; multiplier to get distance 
P1=0 ; start at zero speed 
P2=0 ; start at zero distance 
N10 WHILE (P0 != 0) ; P0=0 is signal to decelerate 
 IF (P1<P6) ; not up to full speed? 
 P1=P1+1 ; increment to increase speed 
 P2=P1*P3 ; distance to travel in segment 
 ENDIF  
 X(P2) ; incremental move segment 
ENDWHILE  
WHILE (P0=0) ; P0=1 is signal to accelerate 
 IF (P1>0) ; still moving? 
 P1=P1-1 ; decrement to decrease speed 
 P2=P1*P3 ; distance to travel in segment 
 ENDIF  
 X(P2) ; incremental move segment 
ENDWHILE  
GOTO 10 ; loops back up when P0=1 again 
CLOSE  
 
Example 18:  Circular Interpolation with Linear Moves 
This example contains subroutines that perform  circular interpolation with blended moves.  The subroutine starting

program must specify the starting point, the ending point, the radius, the direction, and the increment size.  Also, ei-
ther the long-arc/short-arc toggle or the center point must be specified.  Since these specifications are variables that 
hold their value, any that do not change between moves do not have to be re-specified.  The main program in this

PMAC Circular Arc Move Subroutine 
This subroutine performs moves on a circular arc automatically.  The section of the program calling this subroutine 
simply needs to set the following variables as controlling parameters for the move:  
 
Q1:  X-coordinate of the starting point of arc  
Q2:  Y-coordinate of the starting point of arc  
Q3:  X-coordinate of the ending point of arc  
Q4:  Y-coordinate of the ending point of arc  
Q5:  Radius of the arc  
Q6:  0 for counterclockwise 1 for clockwise  
Q7:  0 for short arc 1 for long arc ;-1 if have specified center 
Q8:  subdivide size in degrees  
 
If host has the center location, the following  can be specified also (with Q7=-1) otherwise they will be calculated by 
the routine 
 
Q9:  X-coordinate of the center  
Q10:  Y-coordinate of the center  
 
N10000  ; Circular arc move subroutine 
IF (Q7>-1) GOSUB 20000   ; Must compute center 
Q0=Q1-Q9 ; Prep for ATAN2 
Q26=ATAN2(Q2-Q10) ; Angle from center to start 
Q0=Q3-Q9 ; Prep for ATAN2 
Q27=ATAN2(Q4-Q10) ; Angle from center to end 
IF (Q6=0 AND Q27<Q26) Q27=Q27+360  ; Proper direct. 
IF (Q6=1 AND Q27>Q26) Q27=Q27-360  ; Proper direct. 
IF (Q6=0) ; If counterclockwise 
 Q28=Q26+Q8 ; Increasing angle 
 WHILE (Q28<Q27) ; Not past end angle 
 Q11=Q9+Q5*COS(Q28) ; X-coord on arc 
 Q12=Q10+Q5*SIN(Q28) ; Y-coord on arc 

===== PDF PAGE 518 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-40
 X(Q11)Y(Q12) ; Make partial move 
 Q28=Q28+Q8 ; Increment angle 
 ENDWHILE ; Loop until end angle 
 X(Q3)Y(Q4) ; Make final move 
ELSE ; Clockwise arc 
 Q28=Q26-Q8 ; Decreasing angle 
 WHILE (Q28>Q27) ; Not past end angle 
 Q11=Q9+Q5*COS(Q28) ; X-coord on arc 
 Q12=Q10+Q5*SIN(Q28) ; Y-coord on arc 
 X(Q11)Y(Q12) ; Make partial move 
 Q28=Q28-Q8 ; Decrement angle 
 ENDWHILE ; Loop until end angle 
 X(Q3)Y(Q4) ; Make final move 
ENDIF  
RETURN  
N20000    ; Subroutine to calculate circle center 
  
Q20=SQRT((Q3-Q1)*(Q3-Q1)+(Q4-Q2)*(Q4-Q2)) ; Distance 
Q21=Q5*Q5-Q20*Q20/4  
IF (Q21<0) ; Move distance > 2R: must adjust 
 Q21=0 ; Center on line FR start to end 
 Q5=Q20/2 ; Adjust radius to half distance 
ENDIF  
Q23=SQRT(Q21) ; Distance FR midpoint to center 
Q0=Q3-Q1 ; Prep for ATAN2 
Q24=ATAN2(Q4-Q2) ; Angle from start to end 
Q0=Q20/2 ; Prep for ATAN2 
Q25=ATAN2(Q23) ; Angle of center off mid-line 
IF (Q6=1 AND Q7=1 OR Q6=0 AND Q7=0)  
 Q26=Q24+Q25 ; Add to get ang FR start to cent 
  
ELSE Q26=Q24-Q25 ; Sub to get ang FR start to cent 
Q9=Q1+Q5*COS(Q26)   ; Center X-coord 
Q10=Q2+Q5*SIN(Q26)  ; Center Y-coord 
RETURN  
CLOSE

Example 20: In Position Confirming Routines 
 
While the PMAC has an automatic "in-position" function, it may not meet the exact needs of many users.  It is pos-
sible for these users to construct more sophisticated functions in PLC.  The routines here provide a variety of sug-
gested methods of determining whether a system is "in-position".  Since each user may have a different idea of what 
constitutes a system  settled in position, a variety of techniques are presented here.  These examples are intended to 
provide ideas on how to perform this function both the actual in-position conditions and the action taken on being 
in-position will probably be different in every application (here an output  bit is set). 
 
; ************************* Setup and Definitions ************************  
 ; M-Variable Definitions for Output Bits  
M1->Y:$FFC2,8,1 ; Machine Output 1 
M2->Y:$FFC2,9,1 ; Machine Output 2 
M3->Y:$FFC2,10,1 ; Machine Output 3 
M4->Y:$FFC2,11,1 ; Machine Output 4 
 ; Address bits that show no move is commanded  
M140->Y:$0814,0 ; #1 In-Position Bit 
M240->Y:$08D4,0 ; #2 In-Position Bit 
M340->Y:$0994,0 ; #3 In-Position Bit 
M440->Y:$0A54,0 ; #4 In-Position Bit 
M187->Y:$0817,17 ; &1 In-Position Bit 
M177->* ; Self-referenced variable 
M233->X:$0079,13 ; #2 desired-velocity-zero bit 
M366->X:$00AB,24 ; Motor #3 actual velocity 
M466->X:$00E7,24 ; Motor #4 actual velocity 
;**************** PLC Program to execute In-Position Function************  
OPEN PLC 10  
CLEAR  
 
This first branch is a simple in-position function for motor #1.  Setting an output when the motor becomes "in posi-
tion".  The shadow bit (M177) is used so that the output is set only when the in-position bit first goes true, and will 
not get set again as long as the motor stays in position. 
 
IF (M140=1) ; Motor in position? 
 IF (M177=0) ; Not in position last scan? 
 M1=1 ; Set output 
 M177=1 ; Latch output 
 ENDIF  
ELSE  
 M177=0  
ENDIF  

===== PDF PAGE 521 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-43 
This second branch requires ten consecutive cycles within the in-position 
band to report an "in-position" condition for motor #2 
 
IF (M233=1) ; No commanded move 
 IF (M240=1)  
 P240=P240+1 ; Increment counter 
 IF (P240!<10) ; Ten times in band? 
 P240=10 ; To prevent overflow 
 M2=1 ; Set in-position signal 
 ELSE  
 M2=0 ; Clear in-position signal 
 ENDIF  
 ELSE ; Not in band 
 P240=0 ; Reset counter 
 M2=0 ; Clear in-position signal 
 ENDIF  
ELSE ; Is commanding a move 
 P240=0 ; Reset counter 
 M2=0 ; Clear in-position signal 
ENDIF  
 
This third branch requires that both motors #3 & #4 (in C.S. 1) be in-position and both have moved less than a quar-
ter of the band since the last cycle to set the output. 
 
IF (M187=1)  ; All C.S. 1 motors in position? 
 P366=M366/(I309*32) ; #3 velocity in cts/servo cycle 
 P466=M466/(I409*32) ; #4 velocity in cts/servo cycle 
 IF (P366<(I328/64 AND P466<I428/64) ; Ix28 in 1/16 ct 
 M3=1  
 ENDIF  
ELSE  
 M3=0  
ENDIF

Example 21:  Encoder Modulo Check 
This PLC program uses the position-capture feature of PMAC to do a once-around check of Encoder 1 by triggering 
the capture with the third channel and checking the number of counts that have gone by since the last triggered posi-
tion.  This action should not be started until one C-channel has already been captured. 
 
;******************* Definitions and setup ****************************** 
CLOSE ; To ensure these are on-line 
P50=2000 ; Counts per revolution 
I902=1 ; Capture on rising C-channel 
M40->* ; Flag to control operation 
M41->* ; Error flag 
M103->X:$C003,0,24,S   ; Encoder 1 captured pos reg  
M117->X:$C000,17,1 ; Enc.1 position-captured flag 
CLOSE ; Make sure others are closed 
;********************* PLC Program ************************************** 
OPEN PLC 4 ; Open for editing 
CLEAR ; Erase existing contents 
IF (M40>0) ; User sets M40 to 1 to start 
IF (M40>1 AND M117=1) ; Not 1st time; captured  

===== PDF PAGE 522 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-44
 P12=P11 ; Store from last time thru 
 P11=M103 ; Most recently captured 
 P13=P11-P12 ; Difference between the two 
 IF (P13>P50/2) ; A positive revolution 
 IF (ABS(P13-P50)>1) ; More than 1 off ? 
 M41=1 ; Set error flag 
 ENDIF  
 ELSE  
 IF (P13<-P50/2)  ; A positive revolution 
 IF (ABS(P13+P50)>1)  ; More than one off?  
 M41=1 ; Set error flag 
 ENDIF

 M41=1 ; Set error flag

 M40=2 ; To mark first time done

M41=0 ; Clear error flag to start

Example 22:  Store The Home-Position Encoder Offset 
This program stores the home-position encoder offset for future use.  The encoder position is zero at power-up/reset 
when the home position is found, the motor position is set to zero, but the encoder position is not.  Therefore we will 
want to have an offset value to relate motor and encoder positions if we will be using encoder registers directly for 
position-compare and capture functions (the servo handles the offset automatically for most purposes).  This PLC 
program stores the offset in a P-variable as soon as the position has been found (the capture register will be re-used). 
 
;***************** Set-up and definitions ****************************** 
CLOSE  
M103->X:$C003,0,24,S  ; Enc 1 captured-pos register  
M140->X:$003D,10,1 ; #1 home-search-in-progress 
M141->*

Example 23:  Pure Position Step 
 
This program performs a pure position step on Motor #1.  It is done with the PLC writing directly to the command 
position registers, because motion programs would blend this.  The step size in counts must be in variable P80, and 
the step time (each way) in milliseconds must be in P85.  To run this on a different motor, only the definition of 
M81 must be changed. 
 
CLOSE ; Ensure following are on-line 
DELETE GATHER ; Make sure there is room 
M88->X3,18 ; Data gather prep bit 
M89->X3,19 ; Data gather on bit 
M0->X0,24 ; Servo cycle counter (timer) 
M85->X$07F0,24 ; Open memory for start time 
M86->X$07F1,24 ; Open memory for time elapsed 
M81->D$28 ; #1 cmd. pos. (double word) 
OPEN PLC 2  
CLEAR  
CMD"GAT" ; Turn on data gathering 
P81=P80*I108*32 ; Compute increment to pos reg 
P86=P85*8388608/I10  ; Step time in servo cycle  
M81=M81+P81 ; Increment commanded position 
M85=M0 ; Start of timer 
M86=M0-M85 ; Time elapsed so far 
WHILE (M86<P86) ; Still waiting for specified time? 
 M86=M0-M85 ; Time elapsed so far 
ENDWHILE  
M81=M81-P81 ; Decrement commanded position 
M85=M0 ; Restart timer 
M86=M0-M85 ; Time elapsed so far 
WHILE (M86<P86) ; Past specified time? 
 M86=M0-M85 ; Time elapsed so far 
ENDWHILE  
CMD"ENDGATHER" ; Turn off data gathering 
DISABLE PLC 2 ; Turn self off so no repeat 
CLOSE  
I5=3 ; Make sure PLCs can be enabled 
 ; First, reserve memory for data gathering  
; with the on-line DEFINE GATHER command ( 
; DEF GAT for short).  The step action will be 
; triggered with an "ENABLE PLC 2" command  
; ("ENAPLC2" for short)

Example 28:  Pulsing a Machine Output 
 
This example uses a PLC program to pulse Machine Output 1 every time a distance of 250 counts is passed (vector 
distance) by the axes using Encoders 1 and 2.  The pulse is turned off the next time through the PLC (~1 msec).  
 
;******************* Definitions and setup ******************************* 
M1->Y:$FFC2,8,1 ; Machine Output 1 
M20->* ; Self-referenced flag variable 
M101->X:C001,0,24,S ; 24-bit encoder 1 position 
M201->X:C005,0,24,S ; 24-bit encoder 2 position 
;******************* PLC program contents ******************************* 
CLOSE ; Close any open buffer 
OPEN PLC 2 ; Open buffer for editing 
CLEAR ; Erase old contents 
IF (M20=1) ; M20 sets the mode 
 IF (M1=0) ; Output now off 
 P102=(M101-P101)*(M101-P101) ; X-distance squared  
 P202=(M201-P201)*(M201-P201) ; Y-distance squared 
 IF (SQRT(P102+P202)>250) ; distance > 250?  
 M1=1 ; Set output 
 P101=M101 ; Reset 'last pos' variable 
 P201=M201 ; Ditto 
 ENDIF  
 ELSE  
 M1=0 ; Clear output next time thru 
 ENDIF  
ENDIF  
CLOSE ; Close the buffer 
ENABLE PLC 2 ; Enable the action

Example 30:  Open-loop Movement 
 
This example shows how you can get effective open-loop action during a PMAC motion program.  In open-loop 
mode, the DAC output can be commanded directly.  When used with a current-loop amplifier, this output is a torque 
or force command.  When used with a velocity-loop amplifier, this output is a velocity command.  During this 
"open-loop" action, PMAC is still technically trying to close the position loop.  However, by setting the proportional 
gain to zero, the output of the PID is always zero.  This means that any value written to the output offset I-variable 
(Ix29) is put directly on the DAC.  This is only valid for motors not commutated by PMAC. 
 
What must be handled carefully is the transition in and out of this mode.  Going into "open-loop", the active DAC 
output is copied into the offset variable, and the proportional gain is set to zero (for the smoothest possible transi-
tion).  In addition, the integral gain (Ix33) and integration limit (Ix63) are set to zero so they do not build up, and the 
following error limit (Ix11) is set to zero to disable it.  Coming back into closed loop mode, the actual motor posi-
tion must be copied into a couple of command position registers, one for the motor and one for the axis (scaled), so 
there is no lurch on closing the loop again. 

===== PDF PAGE 529 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-51 
In this example, the loop is closed again in ten steps, ramping down the offset and ramping up the proportional gain.  
This may not be necessary in a particular application -- but the smoothest possible transition was the intent of doing 
the ramping.  Also integral gain and following error limits are restored -- if desired.  This example just uses Motor 
#1 as the X-axis in Coordinate System 1.  The technique is extendible to all motors in all coordinate systems. 
In many cases, this program can be avoided by using the program command "CMD" to send open loop commands 
directly to a motor.  This will be possible if the open motor can be assigned to a coordinate system not running a 
motion program. 
 
;********************* Set-up and Definitions ********************** 
CLOSE  
M102->Y:$C003,8,16,S ; DAC 1 output register 
M162->D:$002C ; Motor #1 actual position register 
M163->D:$080B ; Motor #1 target position register 
M165->L:$081F ; C.S. 1 X-axis scaled target position 
;********************* Example motion program ********************** 
PROG 12  
CLEAR  
WHILE (1<2) ; Infinite loop 
 
This first section of the program is a "dummy" routine to show some closed-loop action.  It does a constant speed 
move. The condition that keeps it in this mode is arbitrary, and would almost certainly be different in an actual ap-
plication. 
 
WHILE (M1=0) ; Stays closed loop until condition false 
INC ; Incremental moves 
TM50  
X100  
ENDWHILE  
 
This portion of the program converts to the "open-loop" mode.  It could easily be put in a subroutine. 
 
DWELL50 ; Make sure stopped 
DWELL50 ; So variables not changed too early 
I129=M102 ; Output offset = DAC output 
I130=0 ; Proportional gain set to zero 
I163=0 ; Integration limit 
I133=0 ; Integral gain 
I111=0 ; Disable following error limit 
 
This portion of the program constitutes the "open-loop" mode.  Note that PMAC thinks it is DWELLing.  During 
this time the host or the PLC can write to I129, changing the open loop output. 
 
WHILE (M1=1) ; Stays in loop until false 
M163=M162 ; Keep making target pos = actual pos 
DWELL10 ; To take up time; could also be other axis moves 
ENDWHILE  
 
This portion of the program converts back to real closed-loop.  It could be put in a subroutine. 
 
M163=M162 ; Motor target position = actual position 
M165=M162/(I108*32) ; Axis scaled target pos = actual pos 
DWELL5 ; Make sure above statements "take"  
DWELL5 ;  before gain is reintroduced 
P129=I129 ; Hold present output value 
P130=8000 ; Increment for prop gain (1/10 of total) 
P131=0 ; Increment counter 
I163=8000000 ; Restore integration limit value 

===== PDF PAGE 530 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-52
I133=50000 ; Restore integral gain 
WHILE (P131<10) ; Loop ten times 
I129=I129-P129/10 ; Decrease by 1/10 of starting value 
I130=I130+P130 ; Increase by 1/10 of target 
P131=P131+1 ; Count the cycle 
DWELL20 ; Control the speed of transition 
ENDWHILE  
I129=0 ; Make sure got proper final value 
I111=32000 ; Restore following. error limit (2000 cts) 
 
This final part of the program DWELLs in real closed loop so the transition can be judged.  Again, the condition 
keeping it in this portion is arbitrary here. 
 
WHILE (M2=0) 
DWELL50 
ENDWHILE 
M2=0 
ENDWHILE 
CLOSE 
 
Example 31:  Inverse Kinematics 
This example shows how PMAC can be used to perform the inverse kinematic problem -- the conversion of user co-
ordinates (usually cartesian) to motor or joint coordinates.  This program works only in two axes -- it shows the con-
version of XY data into radial and angular axes.  This would permit the cartesian specification of points on a rotary 
table with a radial arm.  The concept can be extended to 6 or even 8 axes -- the calculations simply get more in-
volved.  Note that logical branching, not just pure computation, can be done in the conversion (here to handle C-axis 
rollover). 
;********************* Set-up and definitions *********************** 
#3->5000U ; Radial axis definition; units here should 
 ; be the same as for X and Y user units  
#4->13.889C ; Angular (theta) axis definition; units are 
 ; degrees or radians, but must match I15.  
 ; Here 5000 cts/rev yields 13.889 cts/degree. 
I15=0 ; Use degrees in trig calculations. 
Q21=5 ; X zero position in U-axis coordinates 
Q22=0 ; C-axis offset 
 
Program that performs the inverse kinematic problem and actually does the move in joint coordinates.  This is called 
as a subprogram and expects 'X' data (in Q124) and 'Y' data (in Q125).  It converts this data into radius and angle 
coordinates (the inverse kinematic problem) and commands the move -- here of the U (radius) and C (angle) axes.  
Q21 and Q22 should be preset as offsets for the U and C axes, respectively (if needed).  The move is broken into 
small segments and the conversion is done at each segment boundary.  The resulting joint trajectories are then 
splined together so the movement is smooth and accurate. 
CLOSE   
OPEN PROG 500  
CLEAR  
READ(X,Y) ; X endpoint->Q124; Y endpoint->Q125 
Q12=Q10*Q11/1000 ; Distance per segment (user units) 
Q14=Q24 ; X working point is X starting point 
Q15=Q25 ; Y working point is Y starting point 
SPLINE1 ; Cubic spline mode 
TA(Q11) ; Segment time 
Q16=0 ; To start loop 

===== PDF PAGE 531 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-53 
WHILE (Q16<1)  
This section breaks the linear move into small segments.  The coordinate transformation is done at each segment 
boundary.  This next calculation should only be done on "feedrate axes". 
Q34=Q124-Q14 ; X distance to go 
Q35=Q125-Q15 ; Y distance to go 
Q36=SQRT(Q34*Q34+Q35*Q35) ; Vector distance to go  
IF (Q36>Q12) ; Longer than segment size? 
Q37=Q12/Q36 ; Fraction of distance to go 
 
The interpolation below should be done on all axes, feedrate or not 
 
Q14=Q14+Q34*Q37 ; X location at end of next segment 
Q15=Q15+Q35*Q37 ; Y location at end of next segment 
ELSE ; Last segment of move 
Q14=Q124 ; End of segment is end of move 
Q15=Q125 ; End of segment is end of move 
Q24=Q124 ; X starting point for next move 
Q25=Q125 ; Starting point for next move 
Q16=1 ; To mark last segment 
ENDIF  
Now convert to joint coordinates 
 
Q17=Q21-SQRT(Q14*Q14+Q15*Q15) ; Radial axis coordinate  
Q28=Q18 ; Last angular coordinate 
Q0=Q14 ; Second argument for ATAN2 
Q18=ATAN2(Q15)+Q22 ; Angular axis coordinate 
IF (Q18-Q28>180) Q8=Q8-360 ; Rollover going negative 
IF (Q18-Q28<-180) Q8=Q8+360 ; Rollover going positive  
U(Q17)C(Q18+Q8) ; Make segment move 
ENDWHILE  
CLOSE  
 
The following is a sample main program that can use the above program.  This program simply specifies a square in 
user coordinates.  The inverse kinematic problem is basically invisible to it.  This shows that the actual inverse 
kinematics can be largely hidden from the final parts programmer. 
 
OPEN PROG 25  
CLEAR  
Q10=2 ; Desired feedrate (XY units/sec) 
Q11=30 ; Spline piece time 
CALL 500 X2 Y2 ; Move to start of square 
DWELL100  
M1=1 ; Turn on output (e.g. laser) 
CALL 500 X2 Y-2 ; Do first side of square 
DWELL100  
CALL 500 X-2 Y-2 ; Do second side of square 
DWELL100  
CALL 500 X-2 Y2 ; Do third side of square 
DWELL100  
CALL 500 X2 Y2 ; Do last side of square 
DWELL100  
M1=0 ; Turn off output 
CALL 500 X-5 Y0 ; Return to retract position 
CLOSE

3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-54
Start-up data: needed only 
before the first running. 
 
Q24=-Q21 ; Starting X-value 
Q25=-Q22 ; Starting Y-value 
Q8=0 ; Starting C-axis rollover 
Q18=0 ; Starting C-axis 
 
Example 32:  Orientation of a Rotary Head 
This example shows how to orient a rotary head to the angle of movement of an XY system.  The key concept here 
is the use of the ATAN2 function, which returns a value between -180 degrees and +180 degrees.  The ATAN2 
function here takes two arguments: the first is a Y-axis value, and the second is an X-axis value, which is placed in 
the variable Q0 for the coordinate system. 
 
The approach puts the cutting head in a different PMAC coordinate system from the X and Y axes.  This allows it to 
run a separate motion program from the XY system.  The head program can stay the same regardless of what the XY 
program is -- it simply uses the real-time data from the XY system to plan its moves.  This permits the XY program 
to be generated automatically without concern for the details of the head movement.  With the head program resi-
dent in PMAC, head movements are taken care of automatically, working from cues in the XY program. 
 
This example head program looks at two specific cues from the XY program: DWELLs and M1 status.  During an 
XY DWELL, it brings up the head (if it is not up already).  It also issues a '%0' command to the XY coordinate sys-
tem, so the next XY move will not start before the head program is ready.  When the XY DWELL is complete 
(DWELLs are not affected by % commands), the head program looks to see if M1 has been set (the XY program's 
signal for cutter down).  If it has been set, the head program uses the already-calculated XY target positions to com-
pute the required head orientation, moves the head to that angle, lowers the cutter head, then re-starts the XY pro-
gram (with a %100 command). 
 
;********************* Set-up and definitions ********************** 
CLOSE  
I13=10 ; Move segmentation time (msec) 
I15=0 ; Trig functions use degrees 
I427=14400 ; Motor #4 has 14400 cts/rev and will  
; therefore rollover every 14400 cts 
I194=2000000 ; C.S. 1 time base slew rate 
M161->D:$0028 ; Motor #1 present commanded position 
M163->D:$080B ; Motor #1 target position 
M261->D:$0064 ; Motor #2 present commanded position 
M263->D:$08CB ; Motor #2 target position 
M150->X:$0818,0 ; C.S. 1 program-running status bit 
M151->X:$0038,15 ; Motor #1 dwell-in-progress bit 
M1->Y:$FFC2,8 ; Machine Output 1 (PMAC A to D up/down  
; signal) 
&1 ; XY coordinate system 
#1->10000X ; Motor 1 is X axis in C.S. 1 
#2->10000Y ; Motor 2 is Y axis in C.S. 1 
&2  
#3->1000Z ; Motor 3 is Z axis (vertical) in C.S. 2 
#4->40C ; Motor 4 is rotary axis in C.S. 2 (in deg) 
OPEN PROG 2  
CLEAR  
FRAX(Z,C) ; Both vertical and rotary are feedrate  
ABS ; Absolute mode for rollover to work properly 
Q10=I108*32 ; 1 encoder count in Mx61, Mx63 units 
CMD"&1%0" ; Halt C.S. 1 moves temporarily 
F10  

===== PDF PAGE 533 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-55 
C0 ; Move rotary axis to starting position 
DWELL5  
Q2=0 ; Starting angle value 
CMD"&1%100" ; Restore C.S. 1 movement 
WHILE (M150=1) ; As long as XY program is executing 
 IF (M151=1) ; XY dwell in progress 
 CMD "&1%0" ; Keep next XY move from starting 
 F5   
 Z0 ; Pull up cutting head 
 WHILE (M151=1) WAIT  ; Wait for XY dwell to finish 
 IF (M1=1) ; XY program requesting head down? 
 GOSUB 1000 ; Calculate head angle 
 F10  
 C(Q2) ; Rotate head to starting angle 
 Z10 ; Lower head 
 ENDIF  
 DWELL5  
 DWELL5 ; So head up-down move finished 
 CMD"&1%100" ; Allow XY moves to continue 
 ENDIF  
 TM20 ; Set up 20 msec moves 
 WHILE (M150=1 AND M151=0) ; XY program running; no dwell 
 GOSUB 1000 ; Calculate head angle 
 C(Q2) ; Move head to new angle 
 ENDWHILE  
ENDWHILE  
RETURN ; Head program ends when XY program ends 
N1000 ; Start of head angle calculation routine 
Q0=M163-M161 ; X target pos - X current pos 
Q1=M263-M261 ; Y target pos - Y current pos 
IF (ABS(Q0)>Q10 OR ABS(Q1)>Q10) ; target not = current pos ? 
 Q2=ATAN2(Q1) ; Calculate angle -- ATAN2(Q1,Q0) 
ENDIF ; Note that if target pos = current pos 
 ; Q2 does not change 
RETURN  
 
Example 33:  Time Base Following 
This example is for a coil winding machine.  It shows how one axis on PMAC can be used as a master for another 
(or several others) through PMAC's time base following mode.  In this application, Motor #1 (in Coordinate System 
1) is the spindle axis, and is the master axis.  Coordinate System 2 is slaved to the frequency from Motor #1's en-
coder (this encoder is used both for Motor #1's feedback and for Coordinate System 2's master frequency).  Here, 
there is only one axis in C.S. 2: the traversing axis (Motor #3), which moves back and forth axially along the spindle 
to lay down the wire. 
 
The key to proper winding (as for proper threading of screws or other similar applications) is to keep good control of 
the pitch, which requires a proper ratio of traverse speed to spindle speed.  This could be done by writing a single 
coordinated program, but it is difficult to write such a program to keep the axes properly ratioed through the accel-
eration and deceleration of the spindle.  Time-base following lets the program be much simpler: the traverse axis can 
be programmed pretending that the spindle axis is always turning at a fixed ("real-time") frequency, but the program 
executes at a rate proportional to the actual frequency.  What must be done first is to set up the scaling factor to set 
the proper ratio between axes. 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 534 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-56
;********************* Example system parameters ************************ 
;Spindle axis:  
 ; Resolution: 100 lines/rev = 400 cts/rev 
 ; Max speed: 15,000 rpm = 100 cts/msec 
 ; Min slew speed: 100 rpm = 0.667 cts/msec 
 ; "Real-time" frequency = 64 cts/msec (want  
 ; power of 2; want max less than 200%) Scale- 
 ; factor: 131,072/64 = 2048 At "real-time":  
 ; 6.25 msec/rev Traverse axis:  Resolution:

 ; When program starts, this will change to $0729

TS0 ; No S-Curve acceleration

DWELL10 ; before releasing C.S. 2 from slavery

Example 34:  Move Until Trigger 
 
This example shows how to do a registration move, commonly known as a "move until trigger", on PMAC.  It uses 
a position capture register to latch the trigger position immediately.  The program can react to the trigger some time 
later without any loss of accuracy.  In reacting to the trigger, PMAC must take the captured encoder position, con-
vert it to motor position by adding in the home offset (see HOMOFFST.PMC), then scale that to axis position, add-
ing in the desired distance from the trigger position that we wish to stop. 
 
;********************* Set-up and Definitions ************************ 
M103->X:$C003,0,24,S ; Enc 1 captured-position register 
M117->X:$C000,17,1 ; Enc 1 position-captured flag 
I902=2 ; Enc 1 capture on rising flag edge 
I903=0 ; Enc 1 use HMFL1 for capture 
I190=1000 ; Feedrate in units/sec 
M191->L:$0822 ; Motor 1 X-axis coefficient (S.F.) 
M194->L:$0825 ; Motor 1 axis offset 
;************************** Motion Program ***************************** 
OPEN PROG 3  
CLEAR  
ABS ; Absolute move specification 
TA50 ; Accel time to speed 
TS0 ; No S-Curve accel 
F10 ; 10 user units/sec 
P100=5 ; position short of trigger 
X(P100) ; first part of move -- get up to speed 
 ; Now go into loop to look for trigger 
  
TM10 ; Loop time is 10 msec 
TA10 ; Accel time must be <= TM 
P99=M103 ; Ensure it is cleared 
WHILE (M117=0) ; Loop until position captured 
 P100=P100+0.1 ; Increment commanded position 
 X(P100) ; Keep moving 
ENDWHILE ; Found trigger -- calculate destination 

===== PDF PAGE 536 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-58
P104=M103-P103 ; MotorPos=EncPos-HomeOffset 
P105=(P104-M194)/M191 ; AxisPos=(MotorPos-AxisOffset)/S.F. 
 ; Perform final registration move 
TA50  
F10 ; 10 units per second matches old speed 
X(P105+0.75) ; Stop 3/4 unit from trigger 
DWELL100 ; Hold there 
 ; Further action could be taken here 
CLOSE

Example 36:  Motion Program Execution 
 
This program demonstrates how the SAME motion program can be executed asynchronously by 8 different coordi-
nate systems.  It's like having 8 different programs running at the same time, independent of each other.  A PLC 
program monitors the values of M1  through M8.  When any of these variables are set to 1, the corresponding coor-
dinate system executes the program, independent of the other coordinate systems.  When any of these variables set 
to 0, the corresponding coordinate system stops executing, not affecting the other coordinate systems.  In this exam-
ple, the M-variables are self defined, making them behave just like P-variables.  However, you can define these M-
variables to point to machine inputs for reading switches, which can start and stop program execution.

Example 38:  Delayed Program Execution 
 
This program demonstrates how two separate coordinate systems can run the same program with a specified offset 
delay.  In this example, motor 1 in coordinate system 1 will start first, and then motor #2 will follow, lagging by 400 
milliseconds as specified by Q1.  Q-variables are special in PMAC because the same Q-variable can contain unique 
values in different coordinate systems.  Here, Q1=0 in CS 1, and Q1=400 in CS 2.  Also, since both coordinate sys-
tems are running the same program, Q2 is used as the loop counter since it is incremented by both CS 1 AND CS 2-- 
we could not used a P-variable for either the delay variable or the loop counter.  To run the program, Type: ...........  
&1B1R&2B1R  
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 541 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-63 
UNDEFINE ALL        ; Clear out all coordinate system definitions 
&1                  ; Select coordinate system 1 
#1->X               ; Define motor #1 as X 
I190=1000           ; Set feedrate time units to seconds 
Q1=0                ; Set delay variable to 0 msec 
&2                  ; Select coordinate system 2 
#2->X               ; Select coordinate system 2 
I290=1000           ; Set feedrate time units to seconds 
Q1=400              ; Set delay variable to 400 msec 
OPEN PROG 1 CLEAR   ; Open program buffer 1 and clear it out 
Q2=0                ; Set our counter to zero 
ABS                 ; Set absolute mode 
TA100               ; Set acceleration time to 100 msec 
TS0                 ; With no S-curve time 
F10000              ; Set feedrate to 10000 counts/sec 
DELAY (Q1)          ; Delay an amount specified by Q1 in msec 
WHILE (Q2<10)       ; Begin a loop of 10 repetitions 
 X2000           ; Move X 2000 counts 
 DELAY250        ; Delay 250 msec 
 X4000           ; Move X another 2000 counts 
 DELAY250        ; Delay 250 msec 
 X6000           ; Move another 2000 counts 
 DELAY250        ; Delay 250 msec 
 X0              ; Return to position 0 
 DELAY250        ; Delay 250 msec 
 Q2=Q2+1         ; Bump our repetition counter 
ENDWHILE            ; End of loop 
CLOSE               ; Close the program buffer 
 
Example 39:  Integrated Current Limiting 
 
This example shows how a PMAC PLC program can be used to create integrated-current limiting (I2T, "Eye-
Squared-Tee" protection) to supplement or replace that in the amplifier.  This type of protection, as opposed to in-
stantaneous current limiting, is intended to prevent thermal overload of the amplifier and/or motor.  As such, it uses 
a running time average of the square of the current (the digital equivalent of a capacitor charging up and bleeding 
down).  The square function is used because power dissipation is proportional to the square of the current. 
 
This example uses the commanded current output, and so is only valid for current-mode amplifiers.  A more robust 
and flexible version would use the measured current, but that would require an analog to digital converter accessory.  
However, the math and logic are identical in both cases. 
 
;********************* Set-up and definitions ********************** 
CLOSE  
M132->X:0045,8,16,S ; Motor #1 servo loop 16-bit output command -- before 
 ; sent to DACs.  Use of this register permits this  
 ; technique even for PMAC commutated motors. 
P130=16384*16384 ; Squared current limit:  16K*16K bits^2.  When the  
 ; time-averaged current exceeds 16K bits (half of max) 
 ; routine will shut down drive. 
P131=512 ; Number of PLC scans over which the current is averaged.
 ; This number, multiplied by the typical PLC scan cycle 
 ; time, should be approximately equal to the thermal time
 ; constant of the motor. 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 542 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-64
 
;******************* Actual PLC Program ******************************** 
OPEN PLC 1 CLEAR  
P132=0 ; Make sure average is clear to start 
DISABLE PLC 1 ; So only runs once on power-up/reset 
CLOSE  
OPEN PLC 5 CLEAR  
P132=((P131-1)*P132+M132*M132)/P131 ; Compute running average of square 
IF (P132>P130) ; Exceeded limit 
 CMD"&1A" ; Stop any motion in Coordinate System 
 CMD"#1K" ; Kill this motor 
 SEND"Motor1I2T Limit Trapped" ; Message to host 
 M1=1 ; Turn on indicator 
 P132=0 ; Clear running average 
ENDIF  
CLOSE  
Host Example Programs 
 
 
PMACPOLL.C 
 
/* Sample program using read-ready bit polling. 
*/ 
#include <stdio.h> 
#include <dos.h> 
#include <conio.h> 
#define  SERIAL 555 
#define  PCBUS 123 
#define  COM1 1016 
#define  COM2 760 
#define  PMAC_PIC02 528+10 
#define  PMAC_PIC03 528+12 
int combase,     /*base address of the card */ 
 baudrate,      /*baudrate for serial communication */ 
 speed,         /*used for calculating timeout */ 
 able_to_talk,  /*flag for communications established */ 
 timeout;       /*limits how long to look for handshake */ 
char buf [256];     /*holds input string */ 
int config_card_for (int port,int address) { 
 
/* Clock speed multiplier sets limit on how long to look for handshake so read or write can occur.  Software looks 
700 times the number entered for proper handshake before giving up.  The faster the CPU the higher this value 
should be.  For PMAC the only thing this controls is how long to check to see if PMAC is going to send a line or 
not.  For baud rate settings, use the following values: 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 543 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-65 
DESIRED  BAUD RATE VALUE TO USE FOR               
VARIABLE BAUD RATE 
300 Baud rate = 384 
1200 Baud rate = 96 
2400 Baud rate = 48 
4800 Baud rate = 24 
9600 Baud rate = 12 
19200 Baud rate = 6 
38400 Baud rate = 3 
  PMAC is fast enough that the Read Ready bit may only need to be checked at the beginning of the line 
(with timeout provisions) -- once the line read has started, this status check may be superfluous 
 
Make sure you set the E-point jumpers to match your baudrate! */  
speed = 9; 
 combase = address; 
 if (port == SERIAL) { 
  baudrate = 12;               // select 9600 baudrate 
  timeout = 7 * speed * (baudrate + 100); 
  outportb (combase + 3, 131);  /* set up the PC's serial port for communication */ 
  outportb (combase, baudrate); 
  outportb (combase + 1, baudrate/256); 
  outportb (combase + 3, 3); 
 } 
 else {          /* PC-Bus will be used for communication */ 
  baudrate = 0; /* when baudrate is set to 0, PC-Bus communication is assumed */ 
  timeout = 7 * speed * 100; 
  outportb (combase + 5,0) ; 
  outportb (combase + 6,0) ; 
 } 
} 
int sendline (char *outchar) {  /* calls send char to send a string of characters to PMAC 
followed by a CR */ 
 int i = 0; 
 while (outchar [i] != 0) 
  sendchar (outchar [i++]); 
 sendchar (13); 
} 
int sendchar (char outchar) {  /* sends a character to the PMAC-PC card Note: even a 25 MHz 
386 PC has not been able to 'outrun' PMAC, so looking for 
Write Ready bit may be superfluous */ 
 int i; 
 i = 0; 

===== PDF PAGE 544 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-66
 if (baudrate == 0) {  /* Send data over PC-Bus interface */ 
         /* look for Write Ready bit (bit 1 of base address + 2) 
*/ 
  while (i++ < timeout  &&  !(inportb (combase+2) & 2)) ; 
  if (i < timeout) 
   outportb (combase+7, outchar) ; 
 } 
 else {          /* Send data over RS232 interface (serial) */ 
      /* look for Write Ready bit (bit 6 & 5 of base address + 5 & 6) */ 
  while (i++ < timeout && (inportb (combase+5) & 32) == 0); 
  while (i++ < timeout && (inportb (combase+6) & 16) == 0); 
  if (i < timeout) 
   outportb (combase,outchar); 
 } 
 return (0); 
} 
int getline (char *linebuf) { 
/* looks for a line of character data from the PMAC-PC card 
 char ic;

 if (able_to_talk) { 
  ic = nc = i = 0; 
  if (baudrate == 0) {    /* Read data over the PC-Bus interface */ 
   while (i++ < timeout && ic != 13 && nc < 255)

    if ((inportb (combase+2) & 1) == 1) { 
/* found it.. read a character and add on to string */ 
     ic = inportb (combase+7) ; 
     linebuf [nc++] = ic ; 
     i = 0 ; 
    }  
  }  
  else {                 /* Read data over the RS-232 interface */ 
   outportb (combase+4,2);   // release "hold off" signal

    if ((inportb (combase+5) & 1) == 1) { 
     ic = inportb (combase); 
     enable (); 
     linebuf [nc++] = ic; 
     i = 0; 
     disable(); 
     }  
   }  
   outportb (combase+4,0);  // set the "hold off" signal 
   enable ();

   while ((i += 2) < timeout); 
  }  
  linebuf [nc] = 0; 
  return (nc);        /* Return number of characters received */ 
 } 
 else { 
  linebuf [0] = 0; 
  return (0);         /* No characters received! */ 
 } 
}

 n = i = 0; 
 while (n < 3  && i < 11) {

   delay (20); 
   sendchar (26);         /* send ^Z  for serial mode */

  return (1);

PMACINT.C 
 
/* Sample program to talk to PMAC using interrupts.  Make sure jumper E83 for IRQ 5 is in-
stalled to allow PMAC to interrupt the PC at IRQ 5. 
 
*/ 
 
/* ---------------- PMAC bus port addresses --------------- */ 
#define PMACBUFFERSIZE 1024   /* this our queue buffer size */ 
#define PMAC    528   /* bus address of PMAC */ 
#define PMAC_STATUS  PMAC+2  /* bus status byte */ 
#define PMAC_DATA   PMAC+7  /* transmit/receive data */ 
#define PMAC_PIC00  PMAC+8  /* 8259 interrupt controller */ 
#define PMAC_PIC01  PMAC+9  /*     "      "          "    */ 
#define PMAC_PIC02  PMAC+10  /*     "      "          "    */ 
#define PMAC_RECEIVE  2    /* ready to receive bit */ 
#define PMAC_SEND   1    /* ready to send bit */ 
#define PMAC_IS_SENDING (inp (PMAC_STATUS) & PMAC_SEND) 
 
/* ------------ PMAC communication interrupt values ----------------*/ 
#define PMAC_IRQ  4      /* 0-7  IRQ0 - IRQ7 */ 
#define PMAC_MASK  (~(1<<PMAC_IRQ)) /* for unmask of PMAC 8259 */ 
#define PMAC_EOI  0x20     /* Pmac end of interrupt */ 
#define PMAC_IPOS  1      /* IR0 for in position */ 
#define PMAC_BREQ  2      /* IR1 for buffer request */ 
#define PMAC_ERROR 4      /* IR2 for general error */ 
#define PMAC_FERROR 8      /* IR3 for following error */ 
#define PMAC_HREQ  16      /* IR4 for communication */ 
#define PMAC_IR5   32      /* IR5 */ 
#define PMAC_IR6   64      /* IR6 */ 
#define PMAC_IR7   128     /* IR7 */ 
#define PMAC_NOP  0x40     /* 8259 no operation code */ 
 
/*     -------------- PC interrupt values -------------------     */ 
#define IRQ   5     // PC interrupt used for PMAC: 
            // 0 - 15 correspond to IRQ0 - IRQ15 
#if (IRQ < 8)        // interrupt level for XT/AT 
//#define PC_INT   (8+IRQ) 
#define PC_INT  0x77 
#define PC_MASK  (~(1<<IRQ))  // for unmask of PC's 8259 
#define PC_PIC01  0x21    // address for 8259 (master PIC in AT) 
#define PC_PIC00  0x20 
#else                   // interrupt vector for AT only 
#define PC_INT  (104+IRQ) 
#define PC_MASK  (~(1<<(IRQ-8)))// for unmask of PC's 8259

3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-70
#define PC_PIC01  0xA1    // address for second 8259 (slave PIC in AT) 
#define PC_PIC00  0xA0 
#endif 
#define PC_EOI  0x20     // end of interrupt 
#define ACK   0x06 
#define LF    0x0c 
#define EOL    0x0d 
#include <stdio.h> 
#include <dos.h> 
#include <conio.h> 
#include <bios.h> 
static void  (interrupt far *old_comm_int) (); 
static void  interrupt far pmac_comm (); 
static unsigned combase,speed,able_to_talk,timeout,old_int_stat; 
static char  ipos_flag,breq_flag,error_flag,ferror_flag,hreq_flag, 
    ir5_flag,buf [256],comm_buffer [PMACBUFFERSIZE], 
    *current_buffer,*next_in,*next_out; 
void init_pmac_comm () {    /* initialize the PMAC port for interrupt comm. */ 
 setup_pmac_queue (comm_buffer);  /* setup input PMAC queue */ 
 disable ();                      /* disable interrupts until we're done */ 
 old_comm_int = getvect (PC_INT);  /* save original interrupt vector */ 
 setvect (PC_INT, pmac_comm);     /* write in our new interrupt vector! */ 
/* -------  setup PC's 8259...  -------- */ 
 old_int_stat = inp (PC_PIC01); 
 outp (PC_PIC01,(old_int_stat & PC_MASK)); 
/* -------  now setup PMAC's 8259...  -------*/ 
 outp (PMAC, 0);     /* flush PMAC interrupt */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC00, 0x17);  /* 0x17 = edge, 0x1f = level trigger (ICW1) */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0x08);  /* vector for data bus (ICW2) */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0x03);  /* set up for 8086 mode (ICW4) */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0x00);  /* mask out interrupts IR6,IR7 */ 
/* If you wish to enable all interrupt inputs use 0x00 instead of 0xE0 */ 
 outp (PMAC, 0x81);    /* DSP enable read */ 
 enable ();             /* enable interrupts because we're done! */ 
} 
void restore_pmac_comm () {  /*   restore original interrupt vector */ 
 disable (); 
 setvect (PC_INT, old_comm_int); /* replace old PC vectors */ 
 outp (PC_PIC01, old_int_stat); /* restore old status */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0xff);       /* turn off PMAC's 8259 */ 
 enable (); 
} 
static void interrupt far pmac_comm (void) { /* PMAC interrupt service routine */ 
 int     ch; 
 char    isr; 

===== PDF PAGE 549 =====
 3A0-602204-363 
PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-71 
 sound (3000); delay (10); nosound (); /* beep when interrupted! */ 
 disable();                  /* don't be interrupted unitl done */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC02,PMAC_NOP); /* acknowledge interrupt via INTA/ */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC00,0x0A);     /* setup to read IRR register */ 
 isr = inp (PMAC_PIC00);     /* read IRR register */ 
 if (isr & PMAC_IPOS)        /* if IPOS interrupt set, set a flag */ 
  ipos_flag = 1; 
 if (isr & PMAC_BREQ)        /* if BREQ interrupt set, set a flag */ 
  breq_flag = 1; 
 if (isr & PMAC_ERROR)       /* if ERROR interrupt set, set a flag */ 
  error_flag = 1; 
 if (isr & PMAC_FERROR)      /* if FERROR interrupt set, set a flag */ 
  ferror_flag = 1; 
 if (isr & PMAC_HREQ)        /* if HREQ interrupt set, set a flag */ 
  hreq_flag = 1; 
// if (isr & PMAC_IR5) {       /* if IR5 interrupt set, set a flag */ 
  ir5_flag = 1;

 outp(PMAC_PIC02,PMAC_NOP);  /* acknowledge interrupt again! */ 
 outp(PMAC_PIC00,PMAC_EOI);  /* send end-of-intrpt to PMAC's 8259 */ 
 outp(PC_PIC00, PC_EOI);     /* send end-of-intrpt to PC's 8259 */ 
 enable();                   /* re-enable interrupts! */ 
 (*old_comm_int) ();         // jump to replaced routine 
} 
int setup_pmac_queue (char *buf) { 
 next_in = next_out = current_buffer = buf; 
 return (0); 
} 
int read_pmac_queue (char *buf) { /* circular queue buffer for PMAC responses */ 
 int  nc = 0, done = 0; 
 while (!done && (next_in != next_out)) { 
  if (next_out == current_buffer + PMACBUFFERSIZE) 
   next_out = current_buffer; 
        if ((*next_out == EOL) || (*next_out == ACK)) { 
   next_out++; 
   done = 1; 
  }  
        else 
   buf[nc++] = *next_out++; 
 } 
 buf[nc] = 0; 
 return (nc); 
}

int config_card_for (int port,int address) { 
 speed = 9; 
 combase = address; 
 if (port == SERIAL) { 
  baudrate = 12;                /* select 9600 baud */ 
  timeout = 7 * speed * (baudrate + 100); 
  outportb (combase + 3, 131);  /* set up the PC's serial port for 
communication */ 
  outportb (combase, baudrate); 
  outportb (combase + 1, baudrate/256); 
  outportb (combase + 3, 3); 
 } 
 else {          /* PC-Bus will be used for communication */ 
  baudrate = 0; /* when baudrate is set to 0, PC-Bus communication is 
assumed */ 
  timeout = 7 * speed * 100; 
  outportb (combase + 5,0) ; 
  outportb (combase + 6,0) ; 
 } 
}

      aborted = TRUE; 
    }  
    if (!aborted) 
     cprintf ("\r\nDone.\r\n"); 
    else { 
     cprintf ("\r\nAborted.\r\n"); 
     sendline ("CLOSE"); 
    }  
   }  
   else { 
    aborted = TRUE; 
    sound (1000); delay (300); nosound (); 
    cprintf ("\r\nUnable to open file %s",filename); 
   }  
  }  
  fclose (tempfile); 
  sendline ("CLOSE");       /* close rotary buffer */ 
 } 
}

/* PMAC interrupt driven rotary buffer program for PMAC.  Make sure jumper 
E83 for IRQ 5 is installed to allow PMAC to interrupt the PC at IRQ 5. 
 
*/ 
/* ---------------- PMAC bus port addresses --------------- */ 
#define PMACBUFFERSIZE 1024   /* this our queue buffer size */ 
#define PMAC    528   /* bus address of PMAC */ 
#define PMAC_STATUS  PMAC+2  /* bus status byte */ 
#define PMAC_DATA   PMAC+7  /* transmit/receive data */ 
#define PMAC_PIC00  PMAC+8  /* 8259 interrupt controller */ 
#define PMAC_PIC01  PMAC+9  /*  "      "          "    */

#define PMAC_RECEIVE 2    /* ready to receive bit */ 
#define PMAC_SEND   1    /* ready to send bit */ 
#define PMAC_IS_SENDING (inp (PMAC_STATUS) & PMAC_SEND) 
 
/* ------------ PMAC communication interrupt values ----------------*/ 
#define PMAC_IRQ  4      /* 0-7  IRQ0 - IRQ7 */ 
#define PMAC_MASK  (~(1<<PMAC_IRQ)) /* for unmask of PMAC 8259 */ 
#define PMAC_EOI  0x20     /* Pmac end of interrupt */ 
#define PMAC_IPOS  1      /* IR0 for in position */ 
#define PMAC_BREQ  2      /* IR1 for buffer request */ 
#define PMAC_ERROR 4      /* IR2 for general error */ 
#define PMAC_FERROR 8      /* IR3 for following error */ 
#define PMAC_HREQ  16      /* IR4 for communication */ 
#define PMAC_EQU1  32      /* IR5 for DP RAM acknowledge */ 
#define PMAC_NOP  0x40     /* 8259 no operation code */ 
 
/*     -------------- PC interrupt values -------------------     */ 
#define IRQ   5     /* PC interrupt used for PMAC */ 
#define PC_INT  (8+IRQ) 
#define PC_MASK (~(1<<IRQ))  /* for unmask of PC 8259 */ 
#define PC_PIC01 0x21    /* 8259 interrupt controller XT */ 
#define PC_PIC00 0x20    /* " 0-7 interrupts  "    */ 
#define PC_EOI  0x20    /* end of interrupt */ 
#define ACK   0x06 
#define LF   0x0C 
#define EOL   0x0D 
#define PCBUS  123 
#define TRUE  1 
#define FALSE  0

static void  (interrupt far *old_comm_int) ();

void init_pmac_comm () {    /* initialize the PMAC port for interrupt comm. 
*/ 
 disable ();                     /* disable interrupts until we're done */ 
 old_comm_int = getvect (PC_INT);  /* save original interrupt vector */ 
 setvect (PC_INT, pmac_comm);    /* write in our new interrupt vector! */ 
 

===== PDF PAGE 560 =====
3A0-602204-363 
  
 PMAC and PMAC2 Software Reference Manual – Change 1, 25 October 1998 6-82
/* -------  setup PC's 8259...  -------- */ 
 old_int_stat = inp (PC_PIC01); 
 outp (PC_PIC01,(old_int_stat & PC_MASK)); 
 
/* -------  now setup PMAC's 8259...  -------*/ 
 outp (PMAC, 0);    /* flush PMAC interrupt */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC00, 0x17);  /* 0x17 = edge, 0x1f = level trigger (ICW1) */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0x08);  /* vector for data bus               (ICW2) */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0x03);  /* set up for 8086 mode           (ICW4) */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0xFD);  /* mask out ferr,err,ipos,hreq       (OCW1) */ 
 outp (PMAC, 0x81);    /* DSP enable read */ 
 enable ();            /* enable interrupts because we're done! */ 
 breq_flag = 0;        /* clear our interrupt flags */ 
} 
void restore_pmac_comm () {  /* restore original interrupt vector */ 
 disable (); 
 setvect (PC_INT, old_comm_int);  /* replace old PC vectors */ 
 outp (PC_PIC01, old_int_stat);  /* restore old status */ 
 outp (PMAC_PIC01, 0xff);        /* turn off PMAC's 8259 */ 
 enable (); 
} 
 static void interrupt far pmac_comm (void) {/* PMAC interrupt service 
routine */ 
 int  ch; 
 char isr; 
/* sound (3000); delay (10); nosound (); /* beep when interrupted! */ 
 outp(PMAC_PIC02,PMAC_NOP);   /* rising edge of 1st INTA/ pulse */ 
 outp(PMAC_PIC00,PMAC_NOP);   /* trailing edge of 1st INTA/ pulse */ 
 outp(PMAC_PIC02,0x0B);       /* setup to read ISR register */ 
 isr = inp (PMAC_PIC00);      /* read ISR register */ 
 if (isr & PMAC_BREQ)         /* if BREQ interrupt set, set a flag */ 
  breq_flag = 1; 
 outp(PMAC_PIC00,PMAC_NOP);   /* trailing adge of 2nd INTA/ pulse */ 
 outp(PC_PIC00, PC_EOI);      /* send end-of-intrpt to PC's 8259 */ 
 enable();                    /* re-enable interrupts! */ 
}
